Triggers.value: Physical pain in a part of the body

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I pretend it happened to someone else
constantly check body for signs of danger or injury

Threat.value: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger

Negative Appraisals.value: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again
I feel ashamed of what happened to my body

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not
issues.explanation: 'Survival guilt' implies a trauma context involving deaths of others or a mass-casualty/survivor scenario, which is hard to reconcile with the stated index trauma of sexual assault in the absence of any supporting items about others dying. This is a trauma-type mismatch rather than a merely unusual appraisal.

issues.item: Triggers: Feeling Happy: Feeling happy or relaxed
issues.explanation: 'Feeling happy or relaxed' can function as a trigger in PTSD, but here it is weakly integrated with the rest of the profile: the other triggers are perfume/cologne and body pain, while threat is dominated by touch/startle/flashback phenomena and appraisals focus on emotional numbing and self-reliance. The positive-affect trigger is not impossible, but in this item set it lacks a clear clinical link and looks mismatched to the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Threat: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
issues.explanation: The flashback item is not inherently implausible for sexual assault PTSD, but in this profile the rest of the network is strongly organized around hypervigilance to touch/body danger and negative appraisals, with no memory items and no trigger-to-memory/threat linkage in the formulation. A full reliving-style flashback can coexist, but here it sits somewhat at odds with the otherwise body/startle-centered pattern and appears insufficiently supported by the surrounding items.

vignette: Three years ago, Tariq was waiting to change after his evening shift at the downtown gym when a man he did not know followed him into the vacant second-floor locker room. The air grew thick with a sharp, expensive cologne before fingers dug into Tariq's hips and forced him against the cold tile. The man's grip bruised the right side of his torso, and the assault was brief, brutal, and suffocating. Tariq remembers the exact scent, the way his own body had locked up in protest, and the lingering ache in his right ribs that refused to fade. That specific cologne and that particular spot of pain became inextricably tied to the violation, grounding his terror in a physical reality that refused to dissolve. When he returned home, the cologne from the stranger clung to the memory like a stain. Days turned into weeks, and Tariq found himself stopping dead in grocery store aisles or on city sidewalks whenever that same woody, citrus cologne drifted past. His right ribs would throb with a familiar, phantom soreness, a somatic echo that made him press his palms flat against the wall until the sensation passed. What frightened him most was the shame that settled over his skin; he began to view his own body as compromised, a place that had failed him and now bore the mark of what happened to it. He convinced himself he would never feel normal emotions again, that something inside him had been permanently severed. To keep the memories at bay, Tariq stopped thinking about that night entirely. When images tried to surface, he told himself they belonged to a man he once knew, not him. He began constantly checking his torso and shoulders for new injuries or unusual tightness, running his hands over his muscles until he confirmed they were unmarked. The avoidance extended to his marriage. He and his wife, Layla, had always been physically close, but the moment intimacy shifted toward anything resembling the assault, Tariq would pull away. He started making excuses-fatigue, workload, sore muscles-until they grew accustomed to sleeping back-to-back. Over the months, these habits hardened. The clinic where he worked as a physical therapist became a landscape of constant vigilance. During treatment sessions, Tariq found himself monitoring his own posture and breathing as much as his patients', his hands trembling slightly when a patient shifted suddenly in a chair or when a colleague patted his shoulder without warning. He reacted to the unexpected movements and touches with a jolt, his heart hammering against his right ribs, certain that danger was imminent. He could not rely on himself to stay steady, especially when a new client walked in wearing that familiar cologne. He told himself his own body was no longer trustworthy, and that the shame of what had happened to it meant he could not be relied upon to protect his own life or his marriage. The cologne avoidance, the body checks, and the emotional distance simply ran parallel, each occupying his attention. He began turning down double shifts, citing safety concerns when he really meant he could not bear the confined staff rooms. Layla noticed his withdrawal and asked him to speak with someone, but Tariq only felt more certain that he was broken beyond repair. When a junior therapist startled him during a walkthrough, causing him to drop a stack of therapy bands and flinch violently, the illusion of control finally shattered. He booked an appointment that week. Sitting across from the clinician, Tariq clutched his hands together, bracing for the shame he expected, hoping quietly that someone might help him untangle the fear from his own skin before it pulled him entirely under.
